variants.title: Run the decision lifecycle
variants.context: A financial ML system is built in five stages: define the decision contract, reconstruct the evidence that existed at decision time, backtest the full policy, release with bounded authority, then monitor decisions and outcomes. The score is only one part of the decision.
variants.prompt: A payments team wants a fraud score on card authorizations. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Build point-in-time feature rows and labels whose observation windows are explicit and versioned.
Require independent challenge, deterministic limits, reason records, staged exposure, and tested rollback.
Replay model, threshold, review capacity, costs, limits, and delayed outcomes in chronological order.
Join delayed labels, inspect cohorts and regimes, investigate overrides, and contain boundary breaches.
Name the subject, decision timestamp, action, owner, error costs, service target, exclusions, and fallback.

variants.hint: Which stage names the action, and which one earns permission to take it?
variants.explanation: The decision contract comes first because every later stage is evidence about that specific decision.

variants.title: Run the decision lifecycle
variants.context: A financial ML system is built in five stages: define the decision contract, reconstruct the evidence that existed at decision time, backtest the full policy, release with bounded authority, then monitor decisions and outcomes. The score is only one part of the decision.
variants.prompt: An underwriting team proposes a new approval threshold on an unchanged credit score. Put the work in order.

items.text: Rebuild application rows from bureau and ledger values as they stood at each historical decision.
Watch approval, decline, appeal, and loss rates by cohort as the delayed repayment labels mature.
Replay the approval mix, expected loss, calibration, and reason stability over past months in order.
Ship behind independent validation, staged exposure, adverse action reasons, and a tested rollback.
Restate which applications the threshold moves, who owns the action, and what a decline costs the customer.

variants.hint: A threshold change is a policy change, so it needs its own evidence.
variants.explanation: Changing a threshold changes the decision, so the lifecycle runs again even when the model artifact is untouched.

variants.title: Run the decision lifecycle
variants.context: A financial ML system is built in five stages: define the decision contract, reconstruct the evidence that existed at decision time, backtest the full policy, release with bounded authority, then monitor decisions and outcomes. The score is only one part of the decision.
variants.prompt: A desk wants a learned signal to size orders inside existing limits. Put the work in order.

items.text: Replay fees, slippage, market impact, delayed fills, rejects, and position limits across calm and stressed periods.
Release with pre-trade limits outside the model, staged exposure, and a tested kill switch.
Reconstruct book and position values from what was published before each historical order deadline.
Define the order decision, its deadline, the sizing action, the accountable owner, and the no-action fallback.
Monitor fills, rejects, limit breaches, and realized cost by regime after the signal goes live.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what the signal is allowed to command?
variants.explanation: Bounded authority is granted at release, after the replay shows what the policy would have done under real costs.

variants.title: Backtest in order
variants.context: A chronological protocol trains on an earlier interval, leaves a gap when label windows or related events can overlap, evaluates the next contiguous interval, advances the clock across regimes, and locks a final untouched period before selection and live shadowing.
variants.prompt: A team is replacing a random split with a time ordered evaluation. Put the protocol in order.

items.text: Evaluate on the next contiguous interval, keeping related entities off both sides.
Lock a final untouched period before selection, then shadow the full policy on live traffic.
Leave a gap when label windows, features, or related events can overlap the test period.
Advance the clock and repeat across calm, stressed, seasonal, and policy change regimes.
Train on an earlier interval using only feature values available inside that interval.

variants.hint: What has to be true about time between the two sides of a fold?
variants.explanation: Ordered folds with an explicit gap keep later regimes, revised features, and overlapping labels out of training.

variants.title: Backtest in order
variants.context: A chronological protocol trains on an earlier interval, leaves a gap when label windows or related events can overlap, evaluates the next contiguous interval, advances the clock across regimes, and locks a final untouched period before selection and live shadowing.
variants.prompt: Fraud labels mature roughly thirty days after each authorization. Put the protocol in order for that horizon.

items.text: Hold back the most recent month untouched, then run the whole policy in shadow before any customer sees it.
Roll the window forward through a holiday peak and a policy change to see the signal under stress.
Embargo the days whose label windows still reach into the evaluation month.
Fit on authorizations from an earlier month using values published before each authorization.
Score the next contiguous month and keep the same accounts out of both sides.

variants.hint: The label horizon decides how wide the gap has to be.
variants.explanation: The embargo has to cover the label window, otherwise the training month already contains the test month's outcomes.

variants.title: Backtest in order
variants.context: A chronological protocol trains on an earlier interval, leaves a gap when label windows or related events can overlap, evaluates the next contiguous interval, advances the clock across regimes, and locks a final untouched period before selection and live shadowing.
variants.prompt: A researcher has tried nearly two hundred feature and threshold combinations on one dataset. Put the honest protocol in order.

items.text: Walk the folds forward through several regimes rather than reporting the best single window.
Score the next interval and record how many candidates were tried to reach this result.
Insert the gap that keeps overlapping labels and related orders out of the evaluation window.
Judge the finalist on the untouched period that no candidate was ever selected against.
Refit each surviving candidate on an early interval with values available in that interval.

variants.hint: Repeated selection can overfit the backtest itself.
variants.explanation: An untouched final period is the only part of the record that repeated selection has not already consumed.

variants.title: Count the usable evidence
variants.context: A point-in-time row keeps only the values that the production path could already read at the decision deadline. Event time, available time, and recorded time can all differ, so a current warehouse row is not a faithful historical feature row.
variants.prompt: A card authorization is decided at T0. Storage holds an account tenure snapshot available at T minus 180 days, a one hour payment velocity available at T0, a merchant risk snapshot available at T minus 90 minutes, a manual review disposition available at T plus 4 hours, and a chargeback available at T plus 18 days. How many values may enter the feature row?
variants.hint: Compare each available time with the decision deadline.
variants.explanation: Only the three values published by T0 existed for that decision; the review disposition and the chargeback are later label signals.

mistakes.feedback: That is the current warehouse row, which contains values the decision path could not read.
The velocity is available exactly at T0, so it is inside the deadline.

variants.title: Count the usable evidence
variants.context: A point-in-time row keeps only the values that the production path could already read at the decision deadline. Event time, available time, and recorded time can all differ, so a current warehouse row is not a faithful historical feature row.
variants.prompt: A credit application is decided at T0. Storage holds declared income available at T0, a bureau report received at T minus 45 minutes, a corrected bureau report recorded at T plus 3 days, an exposure snapshot available at T minus 6 hours, a verification status available at T minus 10 minutes, a final decision code at T plus 2 minutes, and a first payment outcome at T plus 31 days. How many values may enter the feature row?
variants.hint: A newer version of a field is not automatically the right version.
variants.explanation: The four values published before or at T0 are usable; the correction, the decision code, and the outcome all arrived after the decision.

mistakes.feedback: The corrected bureau report is the newest version of that field but it did not exist at the decision.
That counts every stored value, including the outcome the decision was supposed to predict.

variants.title: Count the usable evidence
variants.context: A point-in-time row keeps only the values that the production path could already read at the decision deadline. Event time, available time, and recorded time can all differ, so a current warehouse row is not a faithful historical feature row.
variants.prompt: An order decision is made at T0. Storage holds the best bid and ask from T minus 8 milliseconds, the current position from T minus 2 milliseconds, the prior session close from T minus 1 day, the execution price from T plus 40 milliseconds, and the next session close from T plus 1 day. How many of these five values must be excluded from the feature row?
variants.hint: Count what arrived after the deadline, not what looks like market data.
variants.explanation: The execution price and the next session close are outcomes of the order, so a row containing them can classify itself.

mistakes.feedback: Two of these values did not exist when the order had to be sent.
The prior session close was published a day before the order, so it is usable evidence.

variants.title: Separate score from authority
variants.context: A score is evidence, not permission. Policy maps the score and context to an action, deterministic limits reject actions outside exposure and eligibility boundaries, and the decision record has to carry specific reasons. Each boundary is versioned and rolled back separately.
variants.prompt: A team wants to ship a new decline threshold by baking it into the model artifact so only one thing is deployed. What is the problem?
options: The artifact becomes slightly larger and slower to load into the serving fleet.
The score distribution changes shape once the threshold moves inside the model.
The threshold and the model can no longer be approved, monitored, or rolled back separately.
optionFeedback: Artifact size is not what makes a bundled policy dangerous.
The threshold does not change the score it is applied to.
Policy is a separate versioned decision, and bundling removes the ability to revert just the policy.
variants.hint: Which of these two things would you want to revert on its own at two in the morning?
variants.explanation: Threshold and policy versions stay outside the model artifact so each can be approved, observed, and rolled back independently.

variants.title: Separate score from authority
variants.context: A score is evidence, not permission. Policy maps the score and context to an action, deterministic limits reject actions outside exposure and eligibility boundaries, and the decision record has to carry specific reasons. Each boundary is versioned and rolled back separately.
variants.prompt: An applicant is declined by a complex model and asks why. The team can produce a feature attribution plot but no stated reasons. What is missing?
options: The applicant should be re-scored with a simpler challenger model to explain the outcome.
The decision system must produce the specific principal reasons and store them with the record.
The model needs to be replaced with a linear model before it can be used at all.
optionFeedback: A second model explains itself, not the decision that was actually taken.
Specific reasons belong to the decision record, produced at decision time and preserved with it.
Model complexity does not remove the obligation to state reasons.
variants.hint: Which artifact has to exist at the moment the decision is made?
variants.explanation: Reason generation is part of the decision system, so the reasons are produced and preserved with each decision, not reconstructed later.

variants.title: Separate score from authority
variants.context: A score is evidence, not permission. Policy maps the score and context to an action, deterministic limits reject actions outside exposure and eligibility boundaries, and the decision record has to carry specific reasons. Each boundary is versioned and rolled back separately.
variants.prompt: A recently validated signal scores an order at very high confidence, but the order exceeds the account's pre-set exposure limit. What should happen?
options: The limit rejects the order, and the rejection is recorded as a control event.
The limit is widened for this order because the signal was validated last week.
The order passes with a warning so the desk can review the breach afterwards.
optionFeedback: Deterministic limits sit outside the learned path so confidence cannot enlarge authority.
Recent validation is not evidence about this order, and it cannot move a risk boundary.
A warning after the fact is not a control, since the exposure was already taken.
variants.hint: Can a control that consults the model still contain the model?
variants.explanation: Hard limits stay independent of model confidence, because leakage, regime change, or integration faults make a confident model wrong.

variants.title: Name the clock
variants.context: Financial records carry several clocks: event time is when it happened, available time is when the decision path could first read it, decision time is the acting deadline, outcome time is when the target event occurred, and recorded time is when a correction or late report reached storage.
variants.prompt: Match each clock to what it marks.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: When the transaction, application, quote, or account change actually occurred.

pairs.label: Available time
pairs.detail: When the production decision path could first read the value after transport and publication.

pairs.label: Decision time
pairs.detail: The deadline at which the system had to act on the case.

pairs.label: Outcome time
pairs.detail: When the target event occurred, such as a chargeback, repayment, or fill.

pairs.label: Recorded time
pairs.detail: When a correction or late report entered storage, which can differ from both other times.

variants.hint: Two of these clocks describe the same value arriving twice.
variants.explanation: Keeping the clocks separate is what makes a historical row reproducible from what the system actually knew.

variants.title: Name the clock
variants.context: Financial records carry several clocks: event time is when it happened, available time is when the decision path could first read it, decision time is the acting deadline, outcome time is when the target event occurred, and recorded time is when a correction or late report reached storage.
variants.prompt: A card authorization is reviewed after a dispute. Match each moment in its history to the clock it belongs to.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: The customer tapped the card at the merchant at 14:02:11.

pairs.label: Available time
pairs.detail: The merchant risk snapshot used for scoring was published at 12:30.

pairs.label: Decision time
pairs.detail: The network required an approve or decline answer within two seconds of 14:02:11.

pairs.label: Outcome time
pairs.detail: The cardholder filed a chargeback eighteen days later.

pairs.label: Recorded time
pairs.detail: A settlement correction for that transaction landed in the warehouse the following week.

variants.hint: Ask which of these the scoring path could have read.
variants.explanation: Only values whose available time precedes the decision time belong in the row; the rest are labels or corrections.

variants.title: Name the clock
variants.context: Financial records carry several clocks: event time is when it happened, available time is when the decision path could first read it, decision time is the acting deadline, outcome time is when the target event occurred, and recorded time is when a correction or late report reached storage.
variants.prompt: A credit application is replayed for a model review. Match each moment to the clock it belongs to.

pairs.label: Event time
pairs.detail: The applicant submitted the form on the third of the month.

pairs.label: Available time
pairs.detail: The bureau report for that application was received forty five minutes before the answer.

pairs.label: Decision time
pairs.detail: The approve, decline, or refer answer was due within the ten minute service target.

pairs.label: Outcome time
pairs.detail: The first payment was missed thirty one days after the account opened.

pairs.label: Recorded time
pairs.detail: A revised bureau file for the same applicant was stored three days after the decision.

variants.hint: The newest version of a field is not always the version that was used.
variants.explanation: Replaying a decision means using the bureau report received for it, not the refreshed file stored afterwards.
